extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Kantian philosophy; scholars of aesthetics and teleology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting Kant's criteria and guiding principles for judging purposiveness, organised beings, and teleology in nature as developed in the Critique of Judgment. Focuses on distinctions (formal/material, relative/inner), definitions (natural purpose, organised being), and maxims for teleological judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement is reflective, not determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: The teleological act of judgement is rightly brought to bear, at least problematically, upon the investigation of nature; but only in order to bring it under principles of observation and inquiry according to the analogy with the causality of purpose, without any pretence to explain it thereby. It belongs therefore to the reflective and not to the determinant judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use teleological judgement as a regulative tool to guide observation and inquiry (analogy with purposive causality), not as a constitutive principle that posits new kinds of natural causality or 'explains' nature. Avoid treating teleology as introducing literal final causes into natural science unless treating it as a heuristic for investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: objective purposiveness merely formal vs material
rubrics_metrics.description: All geometrical figures drawn on a principle display a manifold, oft admired, objective purposiveness; i.e. in reference to their usefulness for the solution of several problems by a single principle. This purposiveness is objective and intellectual but, in this case, merely formal (not real/material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise intellectual/formal purposiveness (e.g., mathematical figures whose unity yields many useful properties) as an a priori feature of our representations that does not imply a material or empirical purpose in objects themselves. Do not conflate formal intellectual purposiveness with empirical purposiveness that would require teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual purposiveness vs aesthetic (subjective) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The purposiveness of mathematical figures is objective and intellectual, not merely subjective and aesthetical. Though we sometimes call certain properties 'beautiful', this is different from the subjective aesthetic purposiveness of the free play of cognitive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish when 'beauty' or purposiveness is a product of intellectual satisfaction (relative perfection, demonstrative elegance) versus when it is an aesthetic, subjective judgment. Avoid broadening 'beauty' to include all intellectual satisfaction, which would make the term indeterminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative (external) purposiveness vs inner (material) purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience leads Judgement to the concept of an objective and material purposiveness only when we judge a relation of cause to effect that appears legitimate only by presupposing the Idea of the effect as the fundamental condition in the cause. Relative purposiveness (utility, advantage for other creatures or humans) is merely external; inner purposiveness is a purpose of the natural being itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating purposiveness, ask whether the purposiveness is merely relative (serving other ends or beings) or an inner purposiveness (constitutive of the being itself). Treat relative purposiveness (e.g., rivers depositing silt useful to humans) as inadequate to establish natural teleology unless the existence of the beneficiary is itself a natural purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: External purposiveness (utility) cannot justify absolute teleological judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective purposiveness based on advantage (utility) is not an objective purposiveness of things in themselves; it is contingent and merely relative. External purposiveness justifies no absolute teleological judgement because it depends on contingent relations and the hypothetical assumption that certain beings' existence is itself a purpose of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that natural processes occur 'for the sake' of humans or other beings merely because they are advantageous. Absolute teleological judgements require further grounds (e.g., inner purposiveness, systemic organisation), not mere external utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for regarding a thing as a natural purpose: contingency of form vis-à-vis natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To see that a thing is only possible as a purpose, its form must be not possible according to mere natural laws, i.e., even empirical knowledge of it as regards cause and effect presupposes concepts of Reason. This contingency of its form in empirical natural laws affords a ground for regarding its causality as possible only through Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute natural purpose when the particular form of an object cannot be accounted for by mere mechanical/natural laws and seems intelligible only by recourse to purposive concepts. Use this criterion cautiously: unusual order alone does not suffice unless the form's possibility resists explanation by known natural mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a natural purpose: thing that is cause and effect of itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisionally: a thing exists as a natural purpose if it is both cause and effect of itself (in a double sense). Examples: (1) a tree produces another tree generically and so perpetuates itself; (2) a tree produces itself individually via growth, using matter which it forms into its own specific organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the reciprocal causality test: does the object both generate and maintain itself (generically and individually)? If so, it qualifies as a candidate for 'natural purpose' (i.e., organised living beings). Consider examples (engrafted buds, parts supporting each other) to test the criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised beings: parts reciprocally cause and are caused by each other
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised being is one in which parts mutually depend upon each other both as to their being and their form, producing a whole by their own causality; conversely the concept of the whole may be regarded as the ground of the form and combination of all the parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish organised beings from machines: machines have moving power but not formative self-propagating power. Look for mutual production, self-repair, and parts existing both as instruments and as things that are produced by the whole. If parts merely serve other parts but do not generate them, the object resembles an artifact rather than an organised natural purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organised beings possess formative self-propagating power (not mere mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised being is not a mere machine (which has merely moving power); it possesses formative power of a self-propagating kind, organising its materials in ways the materials alone could not achieve. This organisational property is not analogous to any physical causality we know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether something is a natural product of teleology, test for formative autonomy: self-production, capacity to repair or maintain itself, and to transform materials into its own specific form. Avoid simplistic analogies between organised beings and artifacts (watches), which miss formative reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle/maxim for judging internal purposiveness in organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: An organised product of nature is one in which every part is reciprocally purpose, end, and means. In such a product nothing is vain, without purpose, or to be ascribed to a blind mechanism of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt this maxim as a regulative principle for investigation: assume that in organisms each part has a role relative to the whole. This maxim guides observation and hypothesis formation in biology (dissection, functional interpretation). But it is a regulative, not constitutive, claim: it directs judgement rather than proving teleological causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical methodological maxim for biologists: 'nothing in such a creature is vain' / 'nothing happens by chance'
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissectors of plants and animals assume as a guiding maxim that nothing in such creatures is vain and that nothing happens by chance; this teleological proposition is used alongside universal physical propositions to guide observation of species and organs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the teleological maxim as a heuristic to drive investigation into functions and internal relations of parts. Be aware it is methodological: it supplies a 'guiding thread' for observation, not a metaphysical proof of purposive causes. Avoid treating it as empirical proof; treat it as a research heuristic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology as a regulative concept for reflective judgement about organised nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of a thing as in itself a natural purpose is not a constitutive concept of Understanding or Reason, but it can serve as a regulative concept for the reflective Judgement, to guide investigation about objects by analogy with our causal purposive activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ teleological concepts to order and systematise inquiry into natural organisms and their relations, while keeping clear that such concepts regulate our cognitive methods rather than constituting literal causal claims about nature's metaphysics. Avoid asserting teleology as an empirical causality unless additional justification is provided.
